VeriLLM: A Lightweight Framework for Publicly Verifiable Decentralized Inference

Decentralized inference is an appealing paradigm for serving large language models (LLMs), offering strong security, high efficiency, and lower operating costs. Yet the permissionless setting admits no a priori trust in participating nodes, making output verifiability a prerequisite for secure deployment.
We present VeriLLM, a publicly verifiable protocol for decentralized LLM inference that (i) achieves security under a one-honest-verifier assumption, (ii) attains near-negligible verification cost (

% of the underlying inference) via a lightweight verification algorithm designed explicitly for LLMs, and (iii) enforces honest checking through a peer-prediction mechanism that mitigates lazy verification in naive voting. We further introduce an isomorphic inference–verification network that multiplexes both roles on the same set of GPU workers. This architecture (i) increases GPU utilization and thereby improves end-to-end throughput for both inference and verification, (ii) expands the effective pool of available validators, strengthening robustness and security, and (iii) enforces task indistinguishability at the worker boundary to prevent job-type–conditioned behavior.

Finally, we provide a formal game-theoretic analysis and prove that, under our incentives, honest inference and verification constitute a Nash equilibrium, ensuring incentive compatibility against rational adversaries. To our knowledge, this is the first decentralized inference verification protocol with an end-to-end game-theoretic security proof.

The rapid rise of Large Language Models (LLMs) stems from their strong utility in various areas, including writing code and creative tasks, leading to rapid adoption in both business and research. However, this success also highlights a key problem with current AI infrastructure: the massive models and computing power needed to run them are concentrated within a few large technology companies. This concentration of core resources creates broad risks, including privacy loss, limited access, single points of failure, and monopolistic control.
In response to these challenges, the paradigm of decentralized inference

offers a promising alternative. By distributing control over data, computational resources, and algorithms across a diverse network of participants, this model inherently promotes greater transparency, fairness, and systemic resilience. It fosters a more competitive innovation landscape by broadening access to foundational AI resources, thereby reducing dependency on centralized gatekeepers and mitigating the risks associated with their concentrated power.

However, a core challenge in this decentralized paradigm is verifiability. In a permissionless network without inherent trust, the system must ensure the correctness of outputs despite potentially faulty or adversarial providers. Without robust verification, participants could respond with arbitrary or incorrect results, severely degrading system reliability. The risk extends beyond mere malfeasance; it includes providers who, in pursuit of cost and efficiency, make opaque optimizations that alter the computational integrity of the model. Common practices—such as using lower numerical precision, compressing the KV-Cache, altering model weights through pruning or distillation, or even modifying input prompts for commercial alignment—can fundamentally change the output in subtle but critical ways

. These undisclosed modifications create significant downstream risks for applications that depend on the deterministic quality of LLM outputs, making independent verification not just a security feature but a prerequisite for trustworthy inference.

Existing approaches to verification—mainly cryptographic proofs and consensus-based replication—face significant practical limitations. Zero-knowledge proof systems can, in principle, attest to the correctness of neural network inference, but current general-purpose and ML-tailored proof systems impose overheads that exceed native inference cost by orders of magnitude for LLMs, especially at realistic sequence lengths and model sizes

. This renders them economically infeasible for high-throughput serving today. Consensus-style schemes replicate inference across multiple nodes and accept majority or supermajority agreement, or employ interactive verification games; these rely on brittle assumptions (e.g., an honest majority, independence of failures, or strong synchrony) and incur substantial excess computation and latency

. Moreover, both families are poorly compatible with modern blockchain environments when public verifiability is required: on-chain verification of large ML proofs remains expensive, deterministic numeric reproducibility across heterogeneous hardware is challenging, and data-availability constraints complicate transparent auditing.

To address these challenges, we present VeriLLM, a novel publicly verifiable protocol for decentralized LLM inference that simultaneously addresses the trilemma of trust assumptions, computational cost, and verification reliability. Our solution provides: (i) security under a one-honest-verifier assumption, eliminating the need for honest-majority models; (ii) near-negligible verification cost (approximately 1% of the underlying inference); and (iii) collusion-resistant verification through a peer-prediction mechanism that prevents lazy validation.
To achieve security under a one-honest-verifier assumption

while keeping costs low, we adopt a hybrid design that combines lightweight empirical rerunning with cryptographic verification-based decisions.
First, all intermediate hidden states are committed to Merkle trees with on-chain root hashes, yielding tamper-evident logs and binding evidence for later checks;
Second, a verifiable random function (VRF) selects unpredictable verification positions, at which any verifier can empirically rerun the corresponding computations off-chain and compare against the committed values; and
Third, a dispute-resolution protocol allows any honest verifier to challenge mismatches by submitting Merkle proofs of inconsistency, with escalation to zero-knowledge proofs when necessary for definitive adjudication.
This hybrid approach keeps typical verification overhead low via sampled reruns, yet guarantees that a single honest verifier can detect and prove misconduct with overwhelming probability.

, we exploit the computational structure of LLM inference. A typical pipeline consists of a Prefill phase followed by a sequential, autoregressive Decoder phase, with the latter constituting the primary computational bottleneck

. We observe that when the complete output sequence is known to verifiers, the expensive Decoder phase can be bypassed: verifiers need only execute the Prefill computation to validate the inference. This approach reduces the verification overhead to a small fraction of the full inference cost.
To achieve public verifiability and prevent lazy verification,

we implement a blockchain-based protocol with an incentive-compatible token economy that preserves system liveness.
First, we adopt a two-layer verification mechanism that minimizes on-chain costs: computationally intensive checks are executed off-chain by selected verifiers, while the blockchain performs lightweight spot checks and adjudicates disputes.
Second, we derive randomness from on-chain commitments to sample positions in the final-token hidden state; for each sample, verifiers submit lightweight on-chain checks (e.g., Merkle openings with minimal recomputation) that attest they actually executed the required computations. A peer-prediction mechanism discourages collusion by rewarding reports that align with the distribution expected from an honest majority.

Building upon this foundation, we replace the traditional heterogeneous Inferencer–Verifier architecture with an isomorphic network in which all GPU workers multiplex both roles. The system no longer distinguishes Inferencer nodes from Verifier nodes, and workers do not distinguish verification tasks from inference tasks; in fact, a worker cannot tell which type of job it is executing. This task indistinguishability at the worker boundary improves security by preventing job-type–conditioned behavior.

Finally, we provide a formal game-theoretic analysis proving that honest inference and verification constitute a Nash equilibrium under our incentive structure, ensuring incentive compatibility against rational adversaries. To our knowledge, this represents the first decentralized inference verification protocol with an end-to-end, game-theoretic security proof, providing strong theoretical foundations for practical deployment in adversarial environments.
We summarize our contributions as follows:
: We establish a novel security model that requires only one honest verifier, achieved through Merkle commitments, VRF-based sampling, and an escalatory dispute resolution protocol.
: We formalize a verification approach requiring only the Prefill phase computation, reducing verification cost to approximately 1% of full inference.
: We introduce an on-chain sampling mechanism with two-layer verification and peer-prediction incentives to ensure validators actually perform computations.
: We propose an isomorphic inference–verification network that co-schedules indistinguishable inference and verification jobs on the same GPU workers.

: We provide a comprehensive security analysis against practical attacks (quantization, early-stop, forged-output) and establish the first formal game-theoretic proof that honest participation constitutes a Nash equilibrium under our incentive mechanisms.

In autoregressive LLMs, causal (left-to-right) attention enforces that the hidden state at position

depends on all preceding tokens, which in turn forces decoding to proceed strictly token by token and limits parallelism. Because the prompt is known a priori, practical systems first run a prefill phase: they compute, in parallel, the representations for all prompt tokens and materialize the key–value (KV) cache, thereby accelerating the subsequent step-wise decode. The same idea applies even more strongly at verification time. Given that the verifier observes the entire sequence (prompt concatenated with the produced output), it can perform a single full-sequence prefill under the causal mask to obtain all token representations in one pass, eliminating the expensive autoregressive decoding loop. Empirically, this reduces the verifier’s computation to roughly
of the original generation time, rendering the verification overhead effectively negligible.

A naïve validation strategy is to have each Verifier re-execute the forward pass under the same model and hyperparameters as the Inferencer and compare the resulting intermediate states against those declared by the Inferencer; the system then aggregates verdicts by majority vote. This baseline, however, creates a lazy-verification incentive: because the Inferencer is honest in the vast majority of cases, a rational Verifier may skip computation and simply report

, quietly eroding security.
We address this with a lightweight commit–sample–check protocol.
Each Verifier posts a binding commitment to its Boolean verdict and hidden states. The contract then draws a set of token indices and requires the Verifier to open the corresponding hidden states on-chain. The contract checks agreement between the openings and the Inferencer’s committed states; a mismatch that contradicts the Verifier’s declared verdict triggers slashing, while consistent openings earn a reward.
Because hidden-state computations exhibit floating-point nondeterminism, the resulting comparisons are unavoidably noisy; consequently, the practical protocol is more intricate. In the following section, we present a noise-robust, secure scheme and provide a game-theoretic analysis of incentives under bounded numerical error.

Conventional consensus protocols assume a majority of honest participants and prove safety under that premise. In contrast, our verification protocol achieves safety under the strictly weaker one-honest-verifier (OHV) assumption; moreover, we show that when verifiers are majority-honest, safety holds even without zero-knowledge proofs. A key difference from consensus is that inference checks involve a randomly sampled, small committee rather than the full network. Consequently, an adversary controlling only a minority of nodes still has non-zero probability of capturing a given committee and biasing a verdict.
We conduct a systematic analysis of this sampling attack and mitigate it through a purpose-designed verifier-selection mechanism together with a reverify scheme.

VeriLLM is a publicly verifiable, decentralized inference system for large language models (LLMs) built atop blockchain. The system comprises three components—(i) a scheduler, (ii) homogeneous node groups, and (iii) on-chain verification contracts—coordinated to deliver auditably correct inference with low verification overhead.

The scheduler orchestrates inference task placement and the logging/forwarding of intermediate hidden states. For each incoming job, it first selects a set of eligible node groups that can jointly serve the task. Within each selected group, it designates one

, with the latter responsible for verifying the former’s outputs. Although logically centralized, the scheduler derives both role assignment and verification checkpoint sampling from a verifiable random function (VRF), ensuring unpredictability and public non-manipulability.

Nodes are organized into groups of homogeneous or near-homogeneous GPU workers.
Owing to GPU memory constraints, each worker may host only a slice of the model.
Concretely, every node in a group hosts an identical copy of the same Transformer block (layer)—including all weights, layer-norm statistics, and kernel configurations.
For any inference job, a node may be assigned as an Inferencer or as a Verifier, as determined by the scheduler.
For each job, a VRF-driven scheduler designates one Inferencer and several Verifiers.
The execution interface and inputs are deliberately role-agnostic. At the onset of Prefill, a worker typically cannot tell whether its computation serves the live inference pipeline or a verification probe. This task-type indistinguishability reduces the opportunity for strategic misbehavior by would-be Verifiers.

A set of on-chain smart contracts that (i) collect verifier-submitted results, (ii) validate these results and finalize them via contract-level consensus, and (iii) dispense incentives accordingly. Participation requires that all roles stake tokens in the contracts, which may be slashed upon adverse outcomes.
(1) A client submits an inference request to the scheduler, which first selects the node groups that can jointly serve the job and then, using a VRF, chooses one

from each group. (2) The Inferencer executes the forward pass in a pipelined manner, streaming intermediate hidden states to the scheduler; the scheduler records these hidden states and forwards them among inference nodes as needed. (3) After inference completes, the scheduler dispatches the corresponding initial hidden states to the assigned Verifiers. Each Verifier runs a prefill computation to reproduce the target hidden states, compares them with the Inferencer’s hidden states, and submits the comparison result to the smart contract on-chain. (4) To deter “lazy” verification, the scheduler samples hidden-state indices; Verifiers must submit the sampled hidden states for on-chain comparison, and the contract rewards or penalizes Verifiers according to the on-chain outcome.

To deter dishonest behavior, both the scheduler and worker nodes must register and lock collateral in on-chain smart contracts. Scheduler registration includes (i) submitting the VRF verification public key so that VRF outputs used for assignment and sampling can be validated, and (ii) publishing a network endpoint to enable node–scheduler communication. Node registration includes (i) declaring the hosted model and the specific layer it serves, and (ii) publishing a reachable endpoint for interaction by the scheduler and peer nodes.

Nodes may deregister to reclaim their stake; withdrawals are subject to a fixed waiting period, allowing the contracts sufficient time to detect and finalize penalties for any misbehavior attributable to the node.

To prevent manipulation of node assignments or HS sampling, all scheduling and sampling decisions are derived from a publicly verifiable random beacon instantiated via a verifiable random function (VRF). The Scheduler’s VRF public key is registered on-chain; every scheduling decision is accompanied by a VRF proof that can be audited off-chain or by smart contracts.

We consider an adversarial environment with potentially malicious Inferencers, Verifiers, and a curious or even Byzantine Scheduler. Smart contracts are assumed correct and executed as specified.
We list the cryptographic assumptions we used as follows:
EUF-CMA security of digital signatures used by nodes.
Collision resistance of hash functions and binding of Merkle commitments.
Unpredictability and unbiasedness of the VRF used for role assignment.
Knowledge of the soundness of any zero-knowledge proofs used to attest signature validity or aggregate Merkle proofs.
We list the system assumptions we used as follows:

At least one verifier per job is honest and online. This is strictly weaker than an honest majority assumption and is sufficient to guarantee safety via either (i) statistical hidden-state comparisons and/or (ii) ZK dispute in the worst case.
Network is eventually synchronous; the contract enforces timeouts and ordering (commit-then-open) to prevent adaptive cheating.
Floating-point nondeterminism is bounded and modeled as small, zero-mean noise; thresholds in our tests are chosen so that honest executions pass with overwhelming probability.
Our scheme provides the following properties.

If all parties follow the protocol and run the prescribed model, then both the offline (full hidden-state) and the on-chain (sampled) checks accept except with negligible probability due to benign numeric noise.

Any materially incorrect inference (wrong model, manipulated states, or premature stop) is detected with high probability by at least one of: (i) the offline full-sequence checks conducted by verifiers, (ii) the on-chain commit-then-sample audit that forces openings of committed values at unpredictable positions, or (iii) the ZK dispute mechanism that allows a single honest verifier to prove an error.

Every relayed hidden state at each segment boundary is bound to a tamper-evident commitment signed by a registered node key; the Scheduler cannot alter states without forging signatures or producing an invalid ZK membership proof.
Sampling indices are derived from commitments fixed prior to seed derivation, preventing adaptive selection of states after seeing the challenge.
Workers receive the same data formats and APIs in inference and verification, removing mode-specific signaling and reducing selective deviation.

(i) Commit-then-open: verifiers must first post a Merkle root of the last token’s hidden state, then later open sampled positions with Merkle proofs. Without actual computation, openings will fail except with negligible probability (due to a hash collision or a lucky guess).
(ii) Task-type indistinguishability: since the verification workload uses the same interface as inference, a prover cannot reliably detect probes and selectively compute.
(iii) Economic design: only verifiers that pass on-chain checks are rewarded; non-openings or failed openings are penalized (slashed). Peer-prediction style aggregation can further deter coordinated guessing by rewarding agreement within the honest cluster and withholding rewards otherwise.
Under Merkle binding and unpredictable sampling, a lazy verifier cannot consistently open correct values and is detected/slashed with overwhelming probability.

If a coalition attempts to submit mutually consistent but fabricated hidden states, the commit-then-sample mechanism forces consistency with the fixed root, but does not alone guarantee semantic correctness. Our design, therefore, (i) requires cross-checks of decoded tokens against hidden states, and (ii) admits a ZK dispute path: any single honest verifier can submit a succinct proof of inconsistency with the prescribed model on a challenged prefix, which the contract verifies. Rewards are skewed to make raising correct disputes strictly profitable.

The Scheduler cannot alter hidden states without forging node signatures or failing ZK membership proofs. Selective exclusion of registered nodes is detectable by recomputing VRF selections once the signatures/VRF proofs are revealed; contracts can slash the Scheduler upon mismatch.

Because commitments are posted on-chain and verifiers are selected via VRF, an adversary must DoS or corrupt all verifiers to prevent detection. Our assumption of at least one honest, live verifier per job suffices to guarantee safety.

Our guarantees rely on at least one honest verifier. A fully colluding ecosystem can still pass statistical checks unless a ZK dispute is mounted. Additionally, the statistical detectors are model- and hardware-calibrated; deploying them on radically different numeric stacks may require retuning the thresholds. Finally, while VRF selection mitigates targeted bias, it cannot prevent the Scheduler from selectively omitting eligible nodes; this is detectable and punishable but not inherently prevented by cryptography.

We empirically measured the divergence of hidden states produced during inference across heterogeneous compute devices (currently tested on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct; additional models are forthcoming). Although floating-point non-determinism across GPU vendors and SKUs introduces small numeric drift, these deviations are limited in magnitude and statistically distinguishable, and consequently, the hidden-state comparison test can, with high probability, determine whether two traces originate from the same underlying model computation.

We further evaluated replacing full-precision models with quantized variants. Hidden states computed by quantized models exhibit substantially larger—and statistically significant—bias relative to the full-precision baseline. Hence, simple statistical tests cleanly separate hidden states from normal inference versus those produced under precision degradation or cheating.

In this paper, we propose VeriLLM, a protocol for verifiable decentralized LLM inference. It achieves efficient and secure verification under a one-honest-verifier assumption and utilizes game-theoretic incentives to ensure that honest participation is a Nash equilibrium.
For future work, we will explore ZK-proofs for stronger collusion resistance, automated threshold calibration for new hardware, and cryptographic mitigations against scheduler censorship.
